messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 26
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Detective
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by romantic partner
  pcl5: 72

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Somatic (Nausea): Feeling nauseous, Visual (Injuries): Visible injuries or wounds on others, Olfactory (Alcohol): Alcohol smell
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Relaxation: avoid relaxing because it feels dangerous, Emotional Numbing: I numb my feelings, Avoid Being Touched: Any form of physical contact with others
  Memory: Auditory Recall: When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event., Vivid Memory: My memories of the frightening event are very clear and detailed., Uncontrolled Access: The memory forces its way into my mind when I do not want it to
  Negative Appraisals: Lost Faith: I have lost my faith in people, life, or a higher power, Outsider: I am permanently an outsider now, Distrust Others: People are not what they seem

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Evan is a 26-year-old detective who came to treatment months after leaving a marriage that, from the outside, had looked stable. He described the violence as something that happened behind closed doors and often after his wife had been drinking. What remained clearest to him was not a single episode but a pattern of nights in which the sharp smell of alcohol reached him before anything else, followed by the sense that he had to read the room perfectly and stay alert. In one assault she struck him hard enough to leave visible injuries, and he remembered registering, with a detached kind of precision, the sight of his own wounds afterward. Even now, when he speaks about it, the memory arrives with unusual clarity. He does not describe it vaguely or as if it were distant; he can hear specific sounds from the event in his head as though they are occurring again in the room with him, and the detail of those moments is so sharp that he sometimes stops mid-sentence when it breaks in against his wishes.

In the weeks after the abuse ended, Evan expected that returning to work and keeping a disciplined routine would steady him. Instead, reminders began appearing everywhere. As a detective, he is frequently around victims, suspects, and crime scenes, and he found himself reacting strongly to visible injuries on other people. A bruised witness, a split lip during an interview, a victim’s bandaged face in the fluorescent light of the precinct—these moments could pull him abruptly out of whatever he was doing. He would feel a wave of nausea rise before he had even fully understood what he was looking at. The smell of alcohol was just as potent. Walking past someone reeking of liquor in a hallway, entering an apartment where stale alcohol hung in the air, or catching it on the breath of someone he was interviewing could change his whole body in an instant. He came to dread that sudden internal shift: the sick feeling in his stomach, the involuntary flood of memory, the sense that the past had forced its way into the present again.

At home, his wife is no longer there, but marriage has not left him feeling connected to anyone. He told the therapist that he has come to believe people are not what they seem, and he says this flatly, not as bitterness but as something he now considers simple fact. What unsettles him most is how fully that belief has spread. It is not just romantic trust that feels damaged; he says he has lost faith in people generally, in life having any basic fairness, and in the idea that there is some benevolent order underneath what happens. He experiences himself as set apart from others now, permanently outside ordinary closeness. When colleagues joke around or talk easily about their weekends, he feels he is imitating normal participation rather than belonging to it.

Over time, he has developed ways of getting through his days that make sense to him but have narrowed his life. He avoids relaxing because letting his guard down feels dangerous. If he comes home exhausted, he keeps the television on, scrolls his phone, or paces instead of settling into the couch or trying to rest. The idea of being calm feels exposed, as though something bad could happen the moment he stopped bracing. He also describes numbing his feelings deliberately. He moves through work with an efficient, shut-down quality that colleagues have noticed, and he prefers that to feeling anything fully. Physical contact has become especially difficult. He avoids being touched in any form, even casual contact that other people would barely notice. At work he steps back if someone reaches for his shoulder, and in his personal life he has become stiff and distant, which has deepened his sense of being separate from everyone else.

What finally brought Evan in was not a single crisis but the accumulation of these moments. He had recently been on a case involving an injured victim, felt nausea almost immediately, and then spent the rest of the day hearing sounds from the abuse in his head while trying to conduct himself professionally. That episode frightened him because it made him feel less in control in the one place he most prides himself on functioning well. He is seeking help now because he does not want every encounter with injury, alcohol, or unwanted closeness to feel hijacked by what happened. At the same time, he is wary of treatment. Part of him is certain that trusting another person is a mistake, and he fears that if he stops holding himself tightly together, he will be left undefended. What he hopes for, though he says it cautiously, is to feel less cut off from life and less ambushed by memories he never invited in.
